newsitem.title: UK: Prodi plays crucial confidence game with market.
newsitem.headline: Prodi plays crucial confidence game with market.

text.p: Italian prime minister Romano Prodi is faced with a chicken or egg dilemma - he needs to convince financial markets Italy will eventually qualify for monetary union in order to make qualification possible.

What may look like an elaborate confidence trick, crucially needs the backing of Italy's European partners to ensure that painful Italian efforts to slash its budget deficits will be rewarded with its inclusion into the single currency if convergence targets are met.
Financial market confidence is proving a powerful weapon because it dictates whether Italy's breakneck deficit reduction enters a vicious or virtuous cicle, economists said.
This is because the servicing of Italy's mountainous public debt, which is more than 120 percent of its gross domestic product, continues to cause Prodi his biggest headache.
These servicing costs are set by the international bond markets, which set the interest rates at which Italy has to pay for existing debt and refunding.

"One reason why there had been growing talk of nine or ten countries in the first wave (of EMU) has been the risk that a sharp back up in Italian rates on any exclusion could push Italy over the edge," said Professor David Currie of the London Business School said at a conference on EMU here this week.
Currie said Italian fiscal policy is very tight and a monetary blowout on top of that would be very damaging. "That can't be in the interests of Germany or France."
Without these astronomical interest payments Italy's budgetary performance is impressive, illustrating the extreme efforts made in recent years to get its finances in order.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) forecasts Italy's primary budget, which excludes interest payments, to be in surplus to the tune of 4.6 percent of its GDP this year. This primary budget has been surplus since 1992.
All the rest of the shortfall, which private analysts believe will likely lead to a total budget deficit of between 3.5 and 4.0 percent of GDP in 1997, is interest payments.

This is why the collapse of Italian long-term interest rates last year, as investors bet on convergence with Germany and the lira's replacement with the euro as soon as 1999, was such a virtuous circle. Lower interest rates meant lower servicing and the less the drain from the public purse.

A reversal of that process now on any exclusion of Italy from EMU could spin it into a polar-opposite vicious circle, making attainment of the 3.0 percent EMU deficit target more difficult in the coming years and eroding market confidence.

"This is why Prodi is talking as much to the markets when making these heartfelt commitments to EMU than he is to Germany or France or even the Italian public," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Italy is busting a gut to make EMU and you've got to say there are internal policy risks if there is no likely reward for that sort of pain," said Meggyesi.

Prodi's implied threat that the lira would be forced to devalue if excluded from EMU is aimed at raising the stakes with Germany and France, which at a time of difficult economnic restructuring and tight fiscal policies would be hit badly by another competitive devaluation by such a major trading partner.
"The impact on the Italian budget and the economy of a back-up in yields and another run on the lira would be huge," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.
"You've got to ask the question whether it is more dangerous for Germany to have an unstable Italy outside EMU or within it as soon as possible."
Yet many analysts say this threat of instability is exactly why Germany wants Italy to remain outside the first wave.

"We are truly moving into the theatre of the absurd when if governments say that exclusion from only the first round of EMU, which is the irrevocable fixing of exchange rates, will mean major exchange rate disruption," said Julian Callow, economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"Italy needs to demonstrate that it is committed to low inflation and sound finances and this will take several years not just one," said Callow.
